name: The Impostor Phenomenon
statement: People who are demonstrably competent can persistently believe their success is a fraud they have not yet been found out for.
statementAccent: a fraud they have not yet been found out for
meaning: An internal experience, not a diagnosis: the sense that one's achievements are the product of luck, timing or having fooled somebody, held by people whose record plainly says otherwise, and unaffected by further achievement.
mechanism: The belief is self-sealing, which is why evidence does not touch it. Success is attributed outward (to luck, to an easy problem, to a generous assessor), so it never accrues to the self; failure is attributed inward and counts fully. Each new achievement therefore raises the stakes rather than the confidence, because it enlarges the gap the person believes will one day be exposed. Clance and Imes described the loop in their original clinical work: sufferers respond either by over-preparing or by procrastinating and then working frantically, succeed either way, and read the success as proof that the effort or the charm (rather than the ability) carried them.

examples.tag: The promotion that makes it worse
examples.text: A senior appointment increases the feeling rather than settling it: more people to disappoint, further to fall, and no reinterpretation of the record that produced it.
Someone prepares far beyond what a task needs, does well, and concludes the preparation was the reason, so the next task needs the same, and the ability is never credited.
Praise is heard as politeness or as the speaker being taken in, which means positive feedback cannot function as evidence at all.

whyItMatters: It named an experience that was widespread, unspoken and assumed to be personal, and naming it is most of what it did — people who believed they were uniquely fraudulent learned the feeling was common. It has become one of the most-searched psychological terms in professional life, which is also why the gap between how it is discussed and what has actually been established about it matters.

working.text: the belief depends on being unique. It survives less well in a room where several people describe the same thing.
record what you thought caused a success at the time, and revisit later. The pattern of crediting everything except your own ability becomes visible in a way it never is in the moment.

working.lead: Separate the feeling from the decision
working.text: the experience is poor evidence about competence, so it is poor input to a decision about whether to apply, speak or take the work.

limits: It is not a clinical diagnosis and appears in neither the DSM-5 nor ICD-11, which leaves prevalence, comorbidity and best practice genuinely unsettled. A 2019 systematic review of 62 studies found that not one had empirically assessed whether any treatment for it works. Measurement is by self-report scales of contested construct validity, and the popular usage has drifted a long way from the original: it now often labels an ordinary, proportionate uncertainty about new work, which is not what Clance and Imes were describing.
misreadings: The preferred term is phenomenon rather than syndrome, because it names an experience a person has and not a disorder they have. It is also not confined to women, despite the original study's population, and it is not the same as low self-esteem or as ordinary self-doubt: the defining feature is the mismatch between an objective record of success and a conviction of fraudulence.
origin: Named by Pauline R. Clance and Suzanne A. Imes in "The Impostor Phenomenon in High Achieving Women: Dynamics and Therapeutic Intervention" (Psychotherapy: Theory, Research & Practice, 1978), from clinical work with high-achieving professional women. Later research found the experience across genders and professions; the 'syndrome' wording is popular usage rather than the authors' term.

sources.text: Clance, P. R. & Imes, S. A. (1978). "The Impostor Phenomenon in High Achieving Women: Dynamics and Therapeutic Intervention." Psychotherapy: Theory, Research & Practice 15(3), 241–247. — the naming paper.

"Impostor syndrome." Wikipedia — the 1978 coinage and population, the phenomenon-not-syndrome distinction, the absence from DSM-5 and ICD-11, and the 2019 systematic review finding none of 62 studies assessed treatment efficacy.
